title: Critical Strip and Critical Line
content: The critical strip $\{s \in \mathbb{C} : 0 < \operatorname{Re}(s) < 1\}$ and critical line $\{s : \operatorname{Re}(s) = 1/2\}$ are the geometric loci central to GRH. The functional equation of $L(s, \chi)$ maps $s \mapsto 1-s$, reflecting the critical strip across the critical line. All known non-trivial zeros lie on the critical line.

title: GRH: Per-Character and Full Statements
content: Two levels of GRH are formalized. `GRH_for_character χ` says all zeros of a single $L(s, \chi)$ in the critical strip lie on the critical line. The full `GRH` quantifies universally: GRH holds for ALL Dirichlet characters of ALL moduli simultaneously. This universal quantification is what makes GRH so powerful — it controls ALL L-functions at once.

title: GRH Right Half Formulation
content: An equivalent formulation: GRH holds iff no $L(s,\chi)$ vanishes with $\operatorname{Re}(s) \in (1/2, 1)$. This 'right-half' form is often more convenient in applications because it directly gives a zero-free region, which is the input needed for contour integration arguments in analytic number theory.

title: GRH ↔ GRH_right_half via Functional Equation
content: The central proved equivalence. The forward direction ($\text{GRH} \implies \text{right half}$) is immediate: zeros on the critical line don't have $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1/2$. The reverse uses the functional equation: if $L(s,\chi) = 0$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s) < 1/2$, then $L(1-s, \chi) = 0$ with $\operatorname{Re}(1-s) > 1/2$, contradicting the right-half hypothesis. So zeros with $\operatorname{Re}(s) < 1/2$ are also excluded, leaving only $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 1/2$.

title: Zero-Free Regions: GRH vs Classical
content: Under GRH, the zero-free region is the entire half-plane $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1/2$ — a dramatic improvement over the classical zero-free region $\operatorname{Re}(s) > 1 - c / \log(q(|t|+2))$, which narrows as the modulus $q$ or height $t$ grows. The classical region approaches $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 1$ logarithmically slowly; GRH gives a fixed boundary at $\operatorname{Re}(s) = 1/2$. This gap is the source of all the quantitative improvements GRH provides.

title: Prime Counting in Arithmetic Progressions
content: The function $\pi(x; q, a)$ counts primes $p \leq x$ with $p \equiv a \pmod{q}$. By Dirichlet's theorem, this grows to infinity when $\gcd(a,q) = 1$. The PNT for APs gives the asymptotic: $\pi(x; q, a) \sim \text{Li}(x)/\varphi(q)$, showing primes distribute equally among the $\varphi(q)$ coprime residue classes.
mathContext:
$\pi(x; q, a) = \#\{p \leq x : p \text{ prime},\; p \equiv a \pmod{q}\}$
$\pi(x; q, a) \sim \frac{\text{Li}(x)}{\varphi(q)} \sim \frac{x}{\varphi(q) \log x}$

title: Siegel-Walfisz vs GRH Error Terms
content: The Siegel-Walfisz theorem gives the unconditional PNT for APs with error $O(x \exp(-c\sqrt{\log x}))$, but only for $q \leq (\log x)^A$. Under GRH, the error shrinks to $O(\sqrt{x} \log x)$ with NO restriction on $q$ vs $x$. The improvement is doubly dramatic: (1) the error term is far smaller ($\sqrt{x}$ vs $x$), and (2) the valid range of $q$ extends all the way to $q < x$. This is the single most important consequence of GRH for prime distribution.
mathContext:
$\text{Siegel-Walfisz}: \left|\pi(x;q,a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)\log x}\right| \leq Cx\,e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}}\quad (q \leq (\log x)^A)$
$\text{GRH}: \left|\pi(x;q,a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)\log x}\right| \leq C\sqrt{x}\log x\quad (q < x)$
prerequisites: prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions

title: GRH Error is Sublinear
content: This theorem proves $\sqrt{x} \log x < x$ for $x > e^4$, confirming the GRH error term is genuinely sublinear. The proof strategy reduces to showing $\log x < \sqrt{x}$, using the identity $\log x = 2 \log \sqrt{x}$ and the standard inequality $\log u < u$. One technical real-analysis bound remains as a sorry.
mathContext:
$\sqrt{x} \cdot \log x < x \quad \text{for } x > e^4$
$\text{Key step: } \log x < \sqrt{x} \text{ for large } x$

title: Linnik's Theorem and GRH Improvement
content: Linnik's theorem (1944) guarantees the least prime in an AP is at most $Cq^L$ for some absolute constants. The best known unconditional exponent is $L \leq 5$ (Xylouris, 2011). Under GRH, this drops to $O(q^2 (\log q)^2)$, i.e., effectively $L = 2$. The theorem `GRH_least_prime_improves_linnik` proves $q^2(\log q)^2 < q^5$ for large $q$, confirming the GRH bound is strictly better. The proof uses $(\log q)^2 < q^3$, which follows from $\log q < q$.
mathContext:
$\text{Linnik}: p_{\min}(q,a) \leq Cq^L \quad (L \leq 5)$
$\text{GRH}: p_{\min}(q,a) \leq Cq^2(\log q)^2$
$\text{Proved: } q^2(\log q)^2 < q^5 \text{ for } q > e$

title: Character Sums: Pólya-Vinogradov and GRH
content: The Pólya-Vinogradov inequality (1918) bounds partial sums of Dirichlet characters: $|\sum_{n=M+1}^{M+N} \chi(n)| \leq c\sqrt{q} \log q$. Under GRH, Montgomery-Vaughan (1977) improved this to $O(\sqrt{q} \log\log q)$ — saving a factor of $\log q / \log\log q$. The theorem `GRH_char_sum_implies_PV` proves $\log\log q \leq \log q$ for $q \geq 3$, confirming the GRH bound is at least as strong.

title: GRH Eliminates Siegel Zeros
content: Siegel zeros are hypothetical real zeros $\beta$ of $L(s, \chi)$ very close to $s = 1$, specifically in $(1 - c/\log q, 1)$. Their possible existence causes the ineffectivity in Siegel's theorem. Since any such $\beta > 1/2$, GRH immediately eliminates them — this is the bridge connecting GRH (OQ02) to the Siegel zero question (OQ01). The theorem `GRH_L_nonzero_right_of_half` goes further: it proves $L(\sigma, \chi) \neq 0$ for ALL $\sigma > 1/2$ by combining GRH (for $1/2 < \sigma < 1$), Dirichlet's nonvanishing ($\sigma = 1$), and the Euler product ($\sigma > 1$).
mathContext:
$\text{Siegel zero: } \beta \in (1 - c/\log q,\, 1),\; L(\beta, \chi) = 0$
$\text{GRH} \implies \beta > 1/2 \implies \text{contradiction}$
$\text{GRH} \implies L(\sigma, \chi) \neq 0 \text{ for all } \sigma > 1/2,\; \chi \neq 1$

title: Effective vs Ineffective Lower Bounds on L(1, χ)
content: Siegel's theorem gives $|L(1, \chi)| \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$, but the constant is ineffective — one cannot compute it. Under GRH, $|L(1, \chi)| \geq C/(\log q)^2$ with an explicit $C$. This effectivity matters enormously: it lets one actually compute bounds in applications to class numbers, least primes, and primality testing. The proof that this implies $\|L(1,\chi)\| > 0$ uses $C > 0$ and $(\log N)^2 > 0$ to bound the ratio away from zero.

title: Class Number Bounds Under GRH
content: For imaginary quadratic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d < 0$, the class number $h(d)$ is linked to $L(1, \chi_d)$ via the Dirichlet class number formula: $h(d) = \frac{\sqrt{|d|}}{\pi} L(1, \chi_d)$. Under GRH, $h(d) \geq C\sqrt{|d|}/\log|d|$ — much stronger than the unconditional Goldfeld-Gross-Zagier bound $h(d) \gg (\log|d|)^{1-\varepsilon}$ from 1983. The gap between $\sqrt{|d|}$ and $\log|d|$ growth is enormous.
mathContext:
$h(d) = \frac{\sqrt{|d|}}{\pi} L(1, \chi_d) \quad \text{(Dirichlet class number formula)}$
$\text{GRH: } h(d) \geq C\frac{\sqrt{|d|}}{\log|d|}$
$\text{Goldfeld-Gross-Zagier: } h(d) \gg (\log|d|)^{1-\varepsilon}$

title: Equivalent Formulations of GRH
content: Three formulations are shown equivalent: (1) the original GRH (all zeros on Re(s) = 1/2), (2) GRH_right_half (no zeros with Re(s) > 1/2), and (3) GRH_via_log_derivative (L'/L has no poles in the right half). The log-derivative formulation is useful because poles of $L'/L$ correspond to zeros of $L$, and the log-derivative appears naturally in the explicit formula connecting primes to zeros.
